extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent examiners, policymakers, academics and students interested in patent subject-matter eligibility (especially gene patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards on whether genetic materials (isolated DNA, cDNA) and related claims are patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, based on the U.S. Supreme Court's Myriad decision and related case law. Useful for advising, prosecuting, examining, or litigating gene-related patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated DNA is not patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated naturally occurring genes are not patent eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court found that Myriad did not 'create anything new' by isolating BRCA1/BRCA2 and concluded isolated DNA is a product of nature and therefore generally patent ineligible. The Court relied on earlier precedent (e.g., Funk Brothers) to hold that mere isolation does not create a new composition of matter. This principle means claims that merely recite 'isolated' natural gene sequences will face §101 invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA can be patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthetically created composite DNA (cDNA) is not a product of nature and therefore is patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treated cDNA as a non-naturally occurring molecule because it is synthetically produced (exons-only strands). However, eligibility may be denied for very short series of DNA without intervening introns if the cDNA is indistinguishable from natural DNA. Drafting and examination should consider structure and similarity to natural sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature doctrine governs §101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention that is a product of nature is not patent eligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that 'genes and the information they encode are not patent eligible under §101 merely because they have been isolated from the surrounding genetic material.' Patentability under §101 hinges on whether the claimed subject matter is a product of nature versus something created by human ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery alone does not satisfy §101 (creation vs discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: A brilliant discovery by itself does not satisfy the §101 inquiry; the inventor must have created something new rather than merely discovered a natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court contrasted Chakrabarty (human-made bacterium patentable) with the mere isolation of genes (not patentable). This criterion focuses on whether human intervention produced a new composition or just isolated what already existed in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short cDNA / indistinguishability exception
rubrics_metrics.description: cDNA may be ineligible where it consists of a very short series of DNA without intervening introns and thus is indistinguishable from natural DNA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if cDNA is generally patent eligible, examiners and drafters should evaluate the length and structure of the claimed cDNA; very short exon-only sequences that are effectively identical to natural sequences may be treated as products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims involving natural phenomena may be ineligible (Mayo influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to natural phenomena or to applying conventional steps to natural relationships (e.g., certain diagnostic methods) can be patent ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court's Mayo decision held that some diagnostic claims that effectively claim laws of nature are ineligible. Although Myriad did not involve method claims (the Court noted respondents used well-established procedures), Mayo remains controlling for method/diagnostic claims and must be considered alongside Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must define sequences more precisely than by saying 'isolated'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims concerning genes may still be patentable if they define the concerned DNA sequences more precisely, or differently, than simply with the word 'isolated'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court's ruling suggests claim drafting should avoid relying solely on 'isolated' language and instead claim novel aspects (e.g., engineered changes, specific, novel sequence features, functional or structural modifications) to survive §101 scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of altered-order DNA not decided
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision did not address the patentability of DNA in which the order of the naturally occurring nucleotides has been altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leaves open that DNA sequences whose nucleotide order has been changed (i.e., engineered/modified sequences) may still be patent eligible, but each must be assessed on whether it is a product of human ingenuity rather than a natural product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency past practice is not dispositive for §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent and Trademark Office's prior practice of awarding gene patents is not entitled to deference in resolving §101 questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court dismissed reliance on PTO historical practice as controlling. Courts will independently assess §101 even if the PTO previously granted similar claims; practitioners should not assume past PTO grants guarantee eligibility.
